title: Chapter 18: A Comparison of Eight Pairs of Companies; Zweig commentary

claims.text: The selected comparisons illustrate valuation questions, not an unbiased test of a stock-selection strategy. Preserve the deliberate selection of cases when using their outcomes.
A strong business can be too expensive and a low-priced business too weak; comparing two stocks does not require buying either.
Normalize unusually favorable conditions before capitalizing earnings, including profits supported by temporary military demand.
Low valuation does not prevent large interim drawdowns. Position sizing and liquidity must survive adverse prices while the underlying thesis is rechecked.
Distinguish accounting growth financed with richly valued shares from durable cash generation; acquisition currency can create a reinforcing price and deal cycle.
Reject the categorical prediction that buying on rising prices must always end in regret. Selected hindsight examples do not establish that every price-based strategy fails.

assimilation: Compare complete claims, earnings quality, capital requirements and price without forcing a trade between arbitrary peers. Preserve successful expensive businesses and unsuccessful cheap ones as counterevidence. Treat anticipated spin-off distributions and takeover values as contingent claims with execution and financing constraints.
adversarial_review: The cases were chosen after results and mix industries, fiscal years, calendar-year returns and different investment horizons. Ball's July 25 earnings disclosure cannot support a July 23 decision. Table 18-1A's 1960 no-dividend entry conflicts with the claimed uninterrupted record; the Air Reduction profitability sentence conflicts with its table. Table 18-4's printed net income, share count and EPS do not reconcile. Cisco's stated decade gain does not imply the stated 217% annual growth. Quarantine these figures instead of silently repairing them. Table 18-10 explicitly uses prices unadjusted for splits; do not compute investment returns from it. Higher revenue need not proportionately deepen losses when margins and fixed costs change. A Palm/3Com apparent arbitrage requires distribution certainty, borrowing availability and financing costs; later prices alone do not demonstrate executable profit. Index inclusion does not guarantee a price rise. Growth and value are neither permanent winners nor mutually exclusive quality categories.
memory_delta: Require both business resilience and price discipline, allow neither-candidate decisions, normalize temporary profits, include dilution and contingent claims, and plan for interim drawdowns. Selected comparisons teach questions, not calibrated return probabilities or universal failure of other strategies.
reading_provenance: Read all PDF pages 412-447 and inspected tables 18-1 through 18-10 and commentary figures 18-1 through 18-4.
